title: Black Death
topic: The Black Death in Europe: how many people died and which places were hit hardest

excerpt.text: The mortality rate of the Black Death in the 14th century was far greater than the worst 20th-century outbreaks of Y. pestis plague, which occurred in India and killed as much as 3% of the population of certain cities.
In 1348, the disease spread so rapidly that nearly a third of the European population perished before any physicians or government authorities had time to reflect upon its origins.
In crowded cities, it was not uncommon for as much as 50% of the population to die.
Half of Paris's population of 100,000 people died.
In Italy, the population of Florence was reduced from between 110,000 and 120,000 inhabitants in 1338 to 50,000 in 1351.

At least 60% of the population of Hamburg and Bremen perished, and a similar percentage of Londoners may have died from the disease as well, leaving a death toll of approximately 62,000 between 1346 and 1353.
Florence's tax records suggest that 80% of the city's population died within four months in 1348.
Before 1350, there were about 170,000 settlements in Germany, and this was reduced by nearly 40,000 by 1450.
The disease bypassed some areas, with the most isolated areas being less vulnerable to contagion.
Plague did not appear in Flanders until the turn of the 15th century, and the impact was less severe on the populations of Hainaut, Finland, northern Germany, and areas of Poland.
Monks, nuns, and priests were especially hard-hit since they cared for people ill with the plague.

variants.text: Since the authorities acted too slowly, it was their fault that so many people died.

The source says: "In crowded cities, it was not uncommon for as much as 50% of the population to die." It speaks of crowded cities only. "All cities" turns a special case into a rule for every city.

"Although" suggests a contrast, but being less vulnerable fits with being bypassed. The wrong connective turns the sentence around. The source says: "The disease bypassed some areas, with the most isolated areas being less vulnerable to contagion."

Here cause and effect are swapped: being bypassed would not make isolated areas less vulnerable. The source does not give this reason: "... with the most isolated areas being less vulnerable to contagion."

variants.text: Since Finland was hit less severely, its people must have been healthier than other Europeans.
variants.explanation: The source says only that the impact was "less severe" there. It gives no reason, and nothing about the health of the people. The conclusion goes beyond the text (an unsupported inference).
Cause and effect are swapped: caring for the sick was the reason for the losses, not their result. The source says: "... especially hard-hit since they cared for people ill with the plague."
Two letters are swapped: "because".

variants.text: It was without doubt the worst catastrophe that Europe has ever suffered.
variants.explanation: "The worst catastrophe" is a judgement, not a counted fact, and "without doubt" presents it as certain. The source gives only numbers and places. This is an opinion stated as a fact.

notes: Source read: English Wikipedia article Black Death, revision 1377102371 (retrieved 2026-10-18); the saved article text (about 13,500 words, references, tables and boxes left out) was read in full. The eleven excerpt sentences come from the section "Consequences", subsection "Deaths" (the last sentence of the paragraph on mass burials and then the paragraph beginning "In 1348, the disease spread so rapidly"). Excerpt sentences, evidence quotes and variant evidence were compared with the saved article text by script (whitespace squeezed); every one occurs in it, in the source's order.

All 15 error classes of the level occur. Classes from grade 7 and from grade 10 are derived, not documented. Misspellings (thrid, tiem, Bremne, monts, nearyl, centruy, sevre, becuase) and real-word errors (grater, cites, Pairs, may of) are constructed on typical English patterns, not taken from a corpus.

The inserted sentences (unfounded blame, generalisation, added claims, unnamed experts, loaded wording, contradiction, unsupported inference, opinion) are invented, harmless and not in the Original; the explanation says so. Place names and figures in the Variante follow the article; Y. pestis is left out of the Variante, and "Y. pestis plague" stays in the Original as the article has it.

Not verified: whether the article's figures are right in the world; they follow the article, not other sources (the article itself gives other estimates elsewhere, e.g. a lower share for Germany and England in a footnote). Sentences of the two paragraphs were left out (never changed), so the excerpt stays within two neighbouring paragraphs.
The source is saved as PDF under public/quellen/en/black-death.pdf (made by the lead) for the mode source.
